lesson.title: Anne Hutchinson and the Antinomian Controversy
lesson.summary: Anne Hutchinson's home meetings and her claim of direct revelation from God challenged the authority of Massachusetts Bay's ministers, leading to a dramatic trial, her banishment in 1637, and the founding of Portsmouth, Rhode Island.
lesson.body:
Anne Hutchinson, born Anne Marbury in England in 1591, emigrated to Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1634 with her husband William and their children, following the Puritan minister John Cotton whose preaching she admired. Educated and unusually well versed in Scripture and theology for a woman of her time, she began holding meetings in her Boston home, at first simply to review and discuss Cotton's recent sermons for women who could not otherwise participate fully in religious debate. The gatherings grew popular, drawing dozens of colonists, including men, and Hutchinson's own theological interpretations increasingly took center stage.

Hutchinson argued that most of the colony's ministers preached a covenant of works, meaning they suggested that good behavior and moral effort helped earn salvation, a position Puritans officially rejected but that crept into everyday preaching about visible signs of grace. She held that only John Cotton and her brother in law John Wheelwright preached the true covenant of grace, in which salvation came from God alone and could not be earned. This dispute, known as the Antinomian Controversy, split the colony's leadership and congregations through 1636 and 1637, threatening the unity that Massachusetts Bay's founders considered essential to their errand into the wilderness.

Governor John Winthrop, alarmed at Hutchinson's growing influence and the challenge it posed to ministerial authority, brought her before the General Court in November 1637. For most of the trial Hutchinson defended herself skillfully, matching her accusers verse for verse and forcing Winthrop into awkward exchanges. Her position weakened only when she testified that she had received direct revelation from God, an immediate personal communication outside the interpretation of Scripture. To Puritan orthodoxy this claim was dangerous because it implied that individuals needed no ministers or texts to know God's will, and it gave the court grounds to convict her.

The court banished Hutchinson, and in March 1638 the Boston church formally excommunicated her as well. Like Roger Williams before her, she found refuge in the emerging settlements around Narragansett Bay. She and her family, along with William Coddington and other supporters, founded Portsmouth on Aquidneck Island in 1638, adding another town to the cluster that would become Rhode Island and reinforcing the colony's growing reputation as a shelter for those Massachusetts Bay would not tolerate.

After William Hutchinson died in 1642, Anne moved with several of her younger children into Dutch territory near what is now the Bronx in New York, partly to escape Massachusetts Bay's continuing claims of authority over the Rhode Island settlements. In August 1643, during a period of conflict between Dutch colonists and Native peoples known as Kieft's War, Hutchinson and most of the family members living with her were killed in an attack by Siwanoy warriors. Her death did not end her influence: the Antinomian Controversy remained a touchstone for later debates in New England over religious authority, the limits of toleration, and the proper relationship between individual conscience and communal order.
